source_text:
τισμὸν, ἤτοι τοῦ νομικοῦ χρόνου τὸ πλήρωμα, καὶ τὸν δυσαχθῆ καὶ βέβηλον τῆς ἁμαρτίας ζυγὸν τῆς ἑαυτῶν ψυχῆς ἀπελάσαντες, μοχθηρίας ἁπάσης ἀποπεπαύμεθα, καλοῦντος ἡμᾶς διὰ πίστεως εἰς τοῦτο τοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ λέγοντος· «Δεῦτε πρός με, πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι, κἀγὼ ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς.» Οὐκοῦν ἀνάπαυσις μὲν, ἡ πρώτη τῆς ἑβδομάδος ἡμέρα, τὸν ἐν ἀρχαῖς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καιρὸν ὑποφαίνουσα. Ἀνάπαυσις δὲ ὁμοίως καὶ ἡ ὀγδόη καθ' ἣν ἀνεβίω Χριστὸς, προσηλώσας τῷ ἰδίῳ σταυρῷ τὸ καθ' ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον, καὶ εἷς ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν, ἵνα ἡμᾶς θανάτου καὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἐξελὼν, ποινῆς ἀπαλλάξῃ καὶ πόνων, καὶ τὴν ἐν ἀρχαῖς ἀνάπαυσιν δι' αὐτοῦ κερδάνωμεν. Τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ πρώτῃ, φησὶ, λήψονται καρπὸν ξύλου ὡραῖον, καὶ κάλλυντρα φοινίκων, καὶ τοὺς ἑτέρους τῶν κλάδων, δι' οὗ παρέσται νοεῖν διακεκραγότος οἱονεὶ τοῦ πράγματος, ὅτι πάλιν ἡμῖν ἐν Χριστῷ τὰς ἐν παραδείσῳ τρυφὰς ἀπονέμει Θεὸς, καίτοι μεταξὺ διωλισθηκόσι διὰ τὴν ἐν ἀρχαῖς παράβασιν. Ἐξεώσμεθα μὲν γὰρ ἐν Ἀδὰμ, ἀλλ' εἰσκεκομίσμεθα διὰ Χριστοῦ. Διεπύθου γάρ που λέγοντος τῷ συγκρεμαμένῳ λῃστῇ· «Ἀμὴν λέγω σοι, σήμερον μετ' ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ.» Δεδυσώπηκε γὰρ ὁ Χριστὸς τὴν στρεφομένην ῥομφαίαν, καὶ ἀνεῖται λοιπὸν τοῖς πεπιστευκόσιν ἡ εἰσδρομὴ, πάντα εἰς τὸ ἐν ἀρχαῖς ἀναμορφοῦντος αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀνασκευάζοντος εἰς τὸ ὅπερ ἦν πάλαι. Ἐκ φυτῶν δὲ τῶν ἀειθαλῶν οἱ κλάδοι, τὸ διηνεκὲς τῆς χάριτος, καὶ τὸ οἱονεί πως ἀμάραντον τῆς ἐλπίδος ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς σημαίνοντες. «Ἀμεταμέλητα γὰρ τὰ χαρίσματα καὶ ἡ κλῆσις τοῦ Θεοῦ,» κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον. Καὶ ἀκατάληκτος ἀληθῶς τῶν ἁγίων ἡ τέρψις. Ἐπιβοήσεται δὲ καὶ ὁ σοφὸς Ἡσαΐας, λέγων· «Εὐφροσύνη αἰώνιος ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς αὐτῶν, αἴνεσις καὶ εὐφροσύνη αἰώνιος καταλήψεται αὐτούς· ἀπέδρα λύπη, ὀδύνη, καὶ στεναγμός.» Παραπεφώνηται δέ πως τοῖς περὶ τῆς ἑορτῆς θεσπίσμασι, τὸ ἐκ χειμάῤῥου εὐφρανθῆναι δεῖν. Ἔφη γὰρ κατὰ τὴν ἐσχάτην τῆς ἑβδομάδος ἡμέραν, ἤτοι κατὰ τὴν ὀγδόην, ἀρύσασθαι μὲν ἐκ χειμάῤῥου τὸ ὕδωρ, εὐφρανθῆναι δὲ οὕτως τοὺς πεπιστευκότας, καὶ χείμαῤῥος δὲ νοητὸς καὶ οὐράνιος ὁ Χριστὸς, τοῖς ἄνωθεν νάμασι τὰς τῶν σεβομένων αὐτὸν κατάρδων ψυχάς. Τοιγάρτοι καὶ ἔφασκε διὰ φωνῆς προφητῶν, «Ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ ἐκκλίνω ἐπ' αὐτοὺς, ὡς ποταμὸς εἰρήνης, καὶ ὡς χειμάῤῥους ἐπικλύζων, δόξαν ἐθνῶν.» Ἀνακεκράγει δέ που καὶ ὁ θεσπέσιος ἡμῖν Δαβὶδ, πρὸς τὸν τῶν ὅλων Θεὸν καὶ Πατέρα· «Ὡς ἐπλήθυνας τὸ ἔλεός σου, ὁ Θεὸς, οἱ δὲ υἱοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐν σκέπῃ τῶν πτερύγων σοῦ ἐλπιοῦσιν. Μεθυσθήσονται ἀπὸ πιότητος οἴκου σου, καὶ τὸν χειμάῤῥουν τρυφῆς σου ποτιεῖς αὐτούς.» Πρέποι γὰρ ἂν καὶ μάλα εἰκότως τοὺς τοῦ παραδείσου πολίτας, τὸ χρῆναι πλουσίως μεταλαχεῖν τοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ ἀμφιλαφέσι τοῦ Πνεύματος κατευφραίνεσθαι χορηγίαις.
{ΠΑΛΛ.} Πρέποι γὰρ ἂν, καὶ ὀρθῶς γε φής.
{ΚΥΡ.} Ἄθρει δὲ ὅπως ἐν τοῖς Ἱεροσολύμοις ἐπετελεῖτο μόνοις ἡ ἑορτὴ, καὶ ἦν πᾶσά πως ἀνάγκη
pass_a_gloss: (after the sabbath-keep)ing in the law, that is, the fullness of the legal time, and having driven away from our own soul the heavy and profane yoke of sin, we have ceased from all wickedness, Christ calling us to this through faith and saying: 'Come to me all those laboring and burdened, and I will give you rest.' So rest is the first day of the week, hinting at the time at the beginnings of man. And likewise rest is also the eighth, on which Christ came back to life, having nailed to his own cross the handwriting against us, and one died on behalf of all, so that taking us out of death and sins he may release us from penalty and toils, and we may gain through him the rest at the beginnings. On the first day, he says, they will take beautiful fruit of a tree, and branches of palms, and the others of the boughs; through which it will be possible to understand, the matter as it were crying out, that God again assigns to us in Christ the delights in paradise, although in between we had slipped away through the transgression at the beginnings. For we were thrust out in Adam, but we have been brought in through Christ. For you heard him somewhere saying to the robber hanging with him: 'Amen I say to you, today with me you will be in paradise.' For Christ has abashed (turned back) the turning sword, and the entry is now let open to those who have believed, he reshaping all things into the condition at the beginning and restoring them to what was of old. And the branches are from ever-flourishing plants, signifying on themselves the continuance of the grace and the as it were unfading of the hope. 'For irrevocable are the gifts and the calling of God', according to what is written. And truly unceasing is the delight of the saints. And the wise Isaiah also will shout, saying: 'Everlasting gladness over their head, praise and everlasting gladness will take hold of them; pain, grief and groaning ran away.' And it has been somehow added to the decrees about the feast that one must rejoice from a torrent. For he said that on the last day of the week, that is on the eighth, (they are) to draw the water from a torrent, and so the believers to rejoice; and a spiritual and heavenly torrent is Christ, watering with the streams from above the souls of those revering him. Therefore also he said through the voice of prophets: 'Behold I incline upon them as a river of peace, and as a torrent flooding, glory of nations.' And somewhere also the divine David cried out for us to the God and Father of all: 'How you multiplied your mercy, O God, and the sons of men will hope in the shelter of your wings. They will be made drunk from the fatness of your house, and you will give them to drink the torrent of your delight.' For it would befit very reasonably the citizens of paradise to partake richly of Christ, and to rejoice in abundant supplies of the Spirit. PALL.: It would befit, and rightly at least you say. CYR.: Observe how the feast was performed in Jerusalem alone, and it was in every way necessity (continues).
pass_b_english: Cyril: …sabbath rest, that is, the fulfillment of the time of the law; and, having driven the heavy and profane yoke of sin away from our own souls, we have ceased from all wickedness, as Christ calls us to this through faith and says, ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest’ (Matthew 11:28). So the first day of the week is rest, and it points to man’s time at the beginning. And the eighth day is likewise rest, the day on which Christ came back to life, having nailed to his own cross the bond that stood against us (Colossians 2:14). One died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14), so that he might take us out of death and sins and free us from punishment and toil, and so that through him we might gain the rest that was at the beginning.

‘On the first day,’ it says, ‘they shall take fine fruit of a tree, and branches of palm trees, and the other boughs’ (Leviticus 23:40). Through this one may understand, as though the thing itself were crying it aloud, that in Christ God again grants us the delights of paradise, though in the meantime we had slipped away from them through the transgression at the beginning. We were thrust out in Adam, but we have been brought back in through Christ. You have heard him, I suppose, saying to the robber who hung beside him, ‘Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise’ (Luke 23:43). For Christ has turned back the turning sword (Genesis 3:24), and the way in now stands open to those who have believed, as he reshapes all things into what they were at the beginning and restores them to what they once were.

The branches come from evergreen plants, and they signify in themselves the unbroken continuance of grace and the unfading, so to speak, quality of our hope. For ‘the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable,’ as it is written (Romans 11:29). And the delight of the saints truly has no end. The wise Isaiah too will cry out, saying, ‘Everlasting gladness shall be over their heads; praise and everlasting gladness shall overtake them; pain, grief and sighing have fled away’ (Isaiah 35:10).

Along with the decrees about the feast, it is somehow added that they must rejoice from the torrent. For he said that on the last day of the week, that is, on the eighth, they were to draw water from the torrent, and that in this way the believers would rejoice. And Christ is a spiritual and heavenly torrent, watering the souls of those who worship him with streams from above. That is why he also said through the voice of the prophets, ‘Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a torrent flooding them with the glory of the nations’ (Isaiah 66:12). Somewhere, too, the inspired David cried out for us to the God and Father of all: ‘How you have multiplied your mercy, O God! The sons of men shall hope in the shelter of your wings. They shall be drunk with the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight’ (Psalm 36:7–8). For it would be very fitting indeed for the citizens of paradise to share richly in Christ and to rejoice in the abundant gifts of the Spirit.
Palladius: Fitting indeed, and you are right.
Cyril: Notice how the feast was kept in Jerusalem alone, and how it was altogether necessary…

choices.english: has turned back the turning sword
choices.why: δυσωπέω, to put out of countenance; the sword of Genesis 3:24 gives way.

choices.english: they must rejoice from the torrent
choices.why: Cyril reads LXX Leviticus 23:40 ('from the brook, to rejoice') as drawing water; kept as he reads it.
